research.abstract: Characium and Characium -like algae represent a taxonomically challenging group within Chlorophyceae. Due to their high phenotypic plasticity and convergent morphology, their true evolutionary relationships have long remained unresolved, and the lack of genomic resources has further hindered taxonomic revision. We sequenced and assembled seven complete chloroplast genomes from Characium and morphologically similar taxa and documented their detailed cell morphology. Comparative genomic analyses revealed that while most genomes retained the typical quadripartite structure, they exhibited significant structural variation, including gene rearrangements and diverse IR expansions/contractions. Furthermore, phylogenetic analyses based on 64 protein-coding genes successfully resolved the long-standing taxonomic ambiguity of Characium and Characium -like algae, placing the strains into three distinct, well-supported clades within Sphaeropleales and Volvocales. The synteny patterns and DCJ distances were consistent with the phylogeny: closely related species showed largely conserved gene order and low DCJ distances, whereas more distant lineages exhibited extensive rearrangements and higher distances. Branch-site tests identified a small set of positively selected genes, mainly related to photosynthesis, proteolysis, and plastid gene expression, suggesting that adaptive processes may have contributed to chloroplast genome diversity in these algae. This study establishes the first clear phylogenomic framework for these lineages, revealing distinct evolutionary patterns of gene loss and structural rearrangement that align with the newly resolved clades. It also provides an important basis for advancing studies on chloroplast genome evolution within Chlorophyceae.

research.abstract: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) presents a significant therapeutic challenge due to increasing multidrug resistance (MDR). While acquired resistance mechanisms are well-documented, the genetic variability of intrinsic efflux pumps like EmrD remains less characterized. This study investigated the genomic diversity and structural conservation of the EmrD transporter in ten clinical MDR isolates from the Kurdistan Region, Iraq. Isolates were screened for the emrD and β-lactamase genes, followed by emrD sequencing, phylogenetic analysis, and in silico protein modeling. Results confirmed the universal presence of emrD alongside multiple resistance genes. Phylogenetic analysis identified notable local genetic diversity, including a highly divergent lineage (DUH 11). Protein modeling mapped non-synonymous substitutions to transmembrane helices 6 and 12, regions critical for the "rocker-switch" conformational changes required for substrate translocation. These findings suggest that while EmrD is a stable component of the MDR machinery, localized genomic divergence may potentially influence efflux efficiency among clinical lineages, warranting future functional validation.

research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) remains the leading infectious killer worldwide. Brazil is among the 30 high-burden TB countries, however, genomic surveillance of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains remains limited. We analyzed a convenience sample of 350 clinical isolates collected between 2016 and 2021 in metropolitan Rio de Janeiro to investigate genomic diversity, drug resistance and transmission dynamics. Among the isolates, 302 were phenotypically susceptible, while 48 showed resistance to at least one drug, including 35 multidrug-resistant (MDR) cases. Whole-genome sequencing predictions showed high concordance with phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (rifampicin 99%, isoniazid 99%, ethambutol 98%, streptomycin 97%). The most common resistance mutations were katG Ser315Thr and rpoB Ser450Leu. All isolates belonged to Lineage 4, predominantly sub-lineages 4.1 (Haarlem) and 4.3 (Latin American-Mediterranean). Despite incomplete sampling, genomic analysis identified 28 transmission clusters involving 23.2% of isolates, including a large MDR-TB cluster in the Tijuca neighborhood. Multi-year clusters indicated continued detection of closely related isolates over time, suggesting the persistence of related genomic lineages. No association was observed between resistance-associated mutations and treatment outcomes, although these analyses were likely underpowered to detect such associations. These findings highlight the need to strengthen genomic surveillance, molecular diagnostics, contact tracing, and treatment follow-up to control TB in the region.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Insomnia (INS) is a major factor determining the risk, severity, treatment resistance and relapse of depression (DEP) and anxiety disorders (ANX), suggesting shared neurobiological vulnerability. Identifying common biological mechanisms that are therapeutically actionable is a foundational step towards improving current clinical care. Since INS, DEP, and ANX share substantial genetic risk, pinpointing the specific genetic factors that influence these three conditions simultaneously offers a route to discover pharmacological targets with transdiagnostic potential. Methods We propose a framework of multi-level trivariate genetic analysis to identify the shared genetic component of INS, DEP and ANX using genome-wide association studies (GWAS). We trace shared components through trivariate genetic overlap, local genetic correlations, overlapping genome-wide significant loci, shared predicted effector genes, and shared putative causal variants. Results We show that INS, DEP and ANX share 55% of their GWAS signal. We identify 195 cross-disorder loci, many of which are likely arising from the same causal variant (at least 50%) or predicted effector gene (60-80%). We find convergence of shared predicted effector genes on biological processes such as inhibitory synaptic transmission, neuronal organization, and axonal development. The majority of shared predicted effector genes that are also druggable are involved in synaptic transmission and located in synaptic membranes, nominating CACNA2D3, DRD2, GRIA1 and GRM5 as key targets for drug development to treat comorbid INS, DEP and ANX. Conclusion These results reveal an interconnected but mechanistically diverse basis for shared genetic liability across co-occurring INS, DEP and ANX, and offer potential candidates for future pathway-tailored transdiagnostic therapeutic targets.

Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis…

research.journal: European Journal of Clinical Microbiology & Infectious Diseases
research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis remains challenging, particularly for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), where invasive sampling, low bacillary burden, and limited sensitivity of nucleic acid-based tests in peripheral specimens hinder timely detection. Here, we report an immunology-driven strategy for biomarker discovery and development of a peptide-based serological assay targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis zinc metalloprotease-1 (Zmp1). Based on the principle that antigenic regions containing overlapping B-cell and CD4⁺T-cell epitopes can promote strong antibody responses through linked recognition and cognate T-cell help, we used an immunoinformatics pipeline to identify two nested immunodominant Zmp1 peptide regions, Mtb-Zp-NT and Mtb-Zp-CT, enriched for overlapping B- and T-cell epitopes.Their diagnostic potential was evaluated using ELISA-based serological assays. A blinded pilot study (N = 137) demonstrated clear discrimination between active TB and TB-recovered individuals. An expanded validation cohort (N = 875), identified from screening approximately 6,086 individuals, included pulmonary TB (PTB), EPTB, TB-recovered individuals, household contacts, non-specific infection/inflammation, and healthy controls. Receiver operating characteristic analyses, supported by DeLong and bootstrap comparisons, demonstrated superior diagnostic performance of the peptide assays compared with Mtb-FL-Zmp1. Mtb-Zp-CT showed the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.93), with > 93% specificity and ~ 76% sensitivity.These findings establish immunologically optimized Zmp1 peptides as promising serological biomarkers for TB, including EPTB. Although further optimization may be required to meet WHO target product profiles, their high specificity supports potential use as an adjunctive diagnostic, particularly for EPTB, and as components of future multi-antigen panels. More broadly, this study demonstrates how mechanistically informed epitope selection can facilitate translation of pathogen-specific immune signatures into minimally invasive diagnostic platforms.

However, the group's diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods: Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes…

research.abstract: Abstract Background The Streptococcus anginosus group (SAG) ( S. anginosus, S. intermedius, and S. constellatus ) causes serious, potentially life-threatening, invasive infections, often in otherwise healthy individuals. However, the group’s diversity is still poorly understood, and with it, the ability to identify prognostic markers of severe disease. Methods Long-read sequencing produced closed genomes for 29 isolates from 25 patients hospitalised primarily for invasive SAG infections, and 21 isolates from 20 non-hospitalised controls. Genomes were classified with GTDB-Tk and combined with 211 reference genomes. After dereplication, 207 SAG genomes (38 isolate, 169 reference) representing 206 strains were analysed using: GTDB classification, average nucleotide identity, multi-marker and core-genome SNP phylogenies, recombination-aware analyses, mobilome, CAZyme and gapseq metabolic profiling, and lineage-aware genome-wide association testing for invasive phenotype. Results Agreement between GTDB-Tk and MALDI-TOF taxonomic classifications was low (42.8%), including two S. massiliensis cases mis-identified by MALDI-TOF as SAG. S. anginosus resolved into four taxa ( S. anginosus , S. hominis , S. whileyi and S. vaginalis ). Phylogenies based on core genome single-nucleotide polymorphisms resolved these species into distinct clades, whereas 16S rRNA gene and multilocus sequence analysis phylogenies did not. The four ex- S. anginosus taxa showed a gradient of genomic cohesion, with S. vaginalis being near-clonal, in contrast to S. anginosus, which shared high levels of sequence ancestry with other neighbouring taxa. Carbohydrate utilisation was strongly lineage-associated, as was propensity for invasive disease. A ∼15Kbp glycosaminoglycan utilisation locus was found in the three taxa of highest disease severity propensity ( S. intermedius, S. constellatus, S. whileyi ) which predicts a direct host glycosaminoglycan feeding mechanism that may contribute to invasive disease. No single functional feature, gene or core-genome SNP was associated with invasiveness however after lineage-adjustment. Combined feature analysis suggests S. vaginalis has undergone a niche restriction and has evolved for a primary existence in the female urogenital tract. Conclusions Under-reported species may be mis-diagnosed as SAG invasive infections. SAG is more diverse than its current three-species definition, with the conventional S. anginosus species proposed to be classed into a complex of four distinct taxa. Invasive capacity appears to be an emergent system-level property rather than from individual features.

research.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of resistance to five new and repurposed drugs (NRDs), identify risk factors for resistance, and characterize associated genetic mutations and transmission among people with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB) in Shenzhen, China. METHODS: Clinical isolates were collected from all people with MDR/RR-TB admitted to Shenzhen Third People's Hospital between January 2022 and December 2024. The minimum inhibitory concentrations of five NRDs - bedaquiline (BDQ), clofazimine (CFZ), delamanid (DLM), pretomanid (PMD) and linezolid (LZD) - were determined using the broth microdilution method. Risk factors for NRD resistance were identified using Firth's penalized logistic regression. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on 99 isolates, including all NRD-resistant strains and randomly selected susceptible strains, to analyze resistance-conferring mutations, phylogeny, and clustering. RESULTS: Among 561 people with MDR/RR-TB, resistance proportions were BDQ 4.3%, CFZ 3.6%, DLM 1.1%, PMD 1.1% and LZD 1.4%. Prior NRD exposure (aOR=4.96; 95% CI, 1.95-12.61; P=0.001) and male gender (aOR=3.64; 95% CI, 1.15-11.56; P=0.028) showed strong positive associations with NRD resistance. BDQ exposure posed a higher risk of both BDQ- and CFZ-resistance than CFZ exposure. Based on the WHO mutation catalogue, WGS predicted NRD resistance with 100% specificity, sensitivity ranged from 16.7% to 75.0%. Notably, 37.5%-66.7% of resistant cases had no prior NRD exposure, and clustered isolates indicated transmitted resistance. CONCLUSION: NRD resistance among MDR/RR-TB patients in Shenzhen remains low. Although prior drug exposure is the primary risk factor, there is also evidence of transmitted resistance. NRD surveillance is essential to guide treatment and control transmission.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tuberculosis caused by members of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) poses significant threats to animal health, public health, and wildlife conservation. Mycobacterium orygis, an emerging MTBC member, remains poorly characterized with respect to its epidemiology and transmission dynamics among Indian wildlife and livestock. METHODS: Fifty-five necropsy tissue samples from 21 captive wild animals were subjected to mycobacterial culture and a panel of molecular diagnostic assays, including multiplex PCR, Xpert-Ultra, and Truenat MTB/Rif. Confirmed MTBC isolates were characterized by drug susceptibility testing (GenoType MTBDRplus) and spoligotyping. Six isolates were selected for whole-genome sequencing (WGS), and phylogenetic analyses were performed against publicly available reference genomes. RESULTS: Of 55 samples, 38 were MTBC-positive and 6 yielded nontuberculous mycobacteria. Drug susceptibility profiling revealed 28 pan-susceptible isolates, nine with isoniazid monoresistance, and one with rifampicin monoresistance. Spoligotyping classified 10 isolates as CAS1-Delhi, 27 as orphan lineages, and one remained unassigned. WGS of six isolates, representing diverse host species and tissue types, identified four as M. tuberculosis (CAS1-Delhi lineage). Notably, one orphan isolate from a blackbuck was reclassified as M. orygis. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that this M. orygis strain was genetically distinct from other Indian wildlife strains and most closely related to a human-derived isolate from Karnataka, suggesting cross-host genomic relatedness. The remaining isolates clustered with Indian and global reference genomes; one was closely related to cattle-derived strains, whereas four were more closely related to human-derived strains. Low pairwise SNP distances (0-78 SNPs) with strong bootstrap support indicated close genomic relatedness across host species and geographic regions. CONCLUSION: This study shows the MTBC genomic diversity among various hosts. The phylogenetic relationships suggest that there is genetic relatedness among host populations such as M. orygis in a captive Indian blackbuck, which was in human contact for a long time. The study demonstrates the importance of integrated One Health genomic surveillance of mycobacterial infections at the human-animal interface and calls for more extensive, epidemiologically linked studies to look for cross-host transmission pathways.

research.abstract: Evaluating a 64-Species, 18-Locus Total-Evidence Supermatrix (L = 31,111 Aligned Columns; 11,436,768 Quartets), 48 Nuclear Functional CDS Orthologs, and 12 Single-Species Regional and Multi-Locus NCBI PopSet Cohorts (N = 432 Isolates) Exclusively via Constrained 100% Native Rust Bio-Suite Combinatorial Optimization (B = 1,000 UFBoot; 25,000 MCMC Generations) We reconstruct the Jurassic-to-Anthropocene global radiation, vector-host co-evolution, and historical demographic dynamics of Anopheles malaria mosquitoes across 544 verified NCBI sequence records comprising a 64-species, 18-locus supermatrix (L = 31,111 aligned columns), 48 nuclear functional coding sequences, and 12 single-species regional and multi-locus NCBI PopSet cohorts (12 × N = 36 = 432 isolates). Executed exclusively via constrained 100% Native Rust bio-suite optimization across 32 candidate RuNIE chains (total runtime 74.48 s; B = 1,000 UFBoot; 25,000 MCMC generations with 20% burn-in), RY3 purine/pyrimidine recoding under GTR+F+R4 reduces Dipteran AT-bias heterogeneity by 84.4% (RCFV = 0.0024 vs. 0.0154, ln L = -339,400.67), dating Crown Culicidae to 194.8 Ma, Crown Anophelinae to 108.4 Ma, the Gondwanan Nyssorhynchus–Cellia split to 78.9 Ma, and the African Gambiae Complex to 4.62 Ma. Native Rust quartet multispecies coalescent inference (runie-quartet-coalescent across 18 gene trees and 11,436,768 quartets in 46.97 ms) resolves 7,414,073 satisfied quartets (normalized Q = 0.6483, mean LPP = 0.8477) while ABBA-BABA tests confirm porous An. gambiae–coluzzii–arabiensis introgression (D = +0.4359 to +0.5177, Z = 12.11–13.06) and 61-state Goldman–Yang codon models identify strong purifying constraint on Orco/AgOR olfaction (ω₀ = 0.056) alongside diversifying selection on TEP1/LRIM1 immunity (ω₂ = 3.23), Anophelin/D7 saliva (ω₂ = 2.66), and VGSC/ACE1/GSTe2 resistance (ω₂ = 2.91). Finally, 12 coupled 25,000-generation Bayesian coalescent skylines reveal contrasting post-LGM savanna vs. Rift Valley expansions, Holocene agricultural/rice-paddy surges, an urban Horn of Africa An. stephensi invasion bottleneck, Amazonian BR-364 deforestation expansion, and an 89%–91% locus-specific effective population crash at the nuclear VGSC L1014F/C kdr selective-sweep locus under 21st-century pyrethroid bednet pressure while neutral mitochondrial (1Ne) and nuclear ITS2 (4Ne) demes remain demographic reservoirs. research.abstract: Abstract Regulatory DNA controls when and where genes are expressed, making it a key driver of phenotypic evolution. Yet detecting selection in non-coding regions remains difficult, as most approaches rely on sequence conservation or changes in substitution rates rather than molecular effects. RegEvol bridges this gap by linking machine learning-based predictions of transcription factor binding to explicit evolutionary models. It uses the distribution of predicted mutational effects to infer fitness functions under different evolutionary scenarios including random drift, stabilising selection, and directional selection. Through maximum-likelihood estimation, it identifies the regime that best explains observed changes along a lineage from an ancestral sequence. When substitution numbers are limited, such as along short evolutionary branches, likelihood differences can be aggregated across sets of regulatory elements to increase statistical power. RegEvol corrects biases that affected previous tests based on machine learning of transcription factor binding, while remaining conservative across different levels of divergence. Applied to over 3 million Drosophila melanogaster regulatory regions, we identify 5.1% under directional selection, enriched near reproductive and immune genes. Applying the aggregation strategy to human CTCF binding across tissues reveals enrichment of directional signals in nervous and male reproductive systems. The framework is readily applicable to experimentally detected regulatory elements with alignable ancestral sequences and is adaptable to future advances in understanding regulatory function, providing a powerful basis for investigating adaptation in non-coding regions.

research.abstract: Wearable accelerometers enable continuous monitoring of physical activity (PA), yet conventional summary measures and population-wide clustering approaches may overlook disease-associated behavioral heterogeneity. Here we introduce LocPA, a computational framework that identifies disease-enriched PA patterns through confounder-adjusted activity profiling, similarity network construction, local disease-enrichment testing and community detection. Applying LocPA to 24-hour accelerometry profiles from the UK Biobank, we identified two recurring PA phenotypes across six diseases spanning cardiometabolic, neurological, psychiatric, renal and cardiovascular conditions: a low-activity phenotype characterized by reduced daytime activity and a sleep-disrupted phenotype characterized by reduced daytime and elevated nocturnal activity. In hypertension and diabetes, the sleep-disrupted phenotype was associated with greater disease burden and less favorable clinical and metabolic profiles, differences not consistently captured by conventional PA summary measures. LocPA also identified disease-specific temporal patterns, particularly in Parkinsons disease. Analyses in an independent National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cohort supported the recurrence of hypertension- and diabetes-enriched patterns across populations and accelerometry measurements. LocPA provides a flexible, disease-driven approach for uncovering clinically relevant temporal PA patterns, with potential applications in disease risk characterization and personalized behavioral interventions.

research.abstract: Abstract Understanding how species diversity originates, accumulates and is sustained across heterogeneous regions is a core goal of macroevolutionary and conservation biology. The genus Huperzia is an ancient and cosmopolitan lineage of lycophytes, with species widely distributed in both temperate alpine and subtropical low‐ to mid‐elevation areas, offering ideal material for investigating the diversification history of early vascular plant lineages. Here, we utilized 87 plastid genomes from 23 species to reconstruct a robust phylogenetic framework within Huperzia and found that the development of the petiole and midrib should be considered supplementary diagnostic characters in future taxonomic revisions. Our spatiotemporal and spatial phylogenetic analyses indicated that temperate and montane regions, especially northeastern China and parts of the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau, preserve phylogenetically distinctive paleo‐lineages, whereas subtropical evergreen broad‐leaved forests contain younger lineages associated with ecological expansion and trait differentiation. This niche transition was accompanied by repeated leaf‐trait differentiation and shifts in plastid‐gene selection in subtropical lineages, with three positively selected genes ( rps19 , chlB and atpH ) identified by branch‐site analyses. This evolutionary strategy provides a new perspective for understanding how early vascular plants maintained a dynamic equilibrium between refugial conservatism and adaptive innovation.

items.title: Molecular characterisation of a Klebsiella pneumoniae neonatal sepsis outbreak in a rural Gambian hospital: a retrospective genomic epidemiology investigation
items.summary: BackgroundKlebsiella pneumoniae is a common cause of neonatal sepsis in Africa, and is frequently hospital acquired. We recently reported an outbreak of multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae sepsis amongst neonates at a rural hospital in The Gambia, West Africa, involving 57 cases and case fatality of 60%. Here we undertook a retrospective pathogen genomic epidemiology study of clinical and…

research.abstract: Abstract Background Klebsiella pneumoniae is a common cause of neonatal sepsis in Africa, and is frequently hospital acquired. We recently reported an outbreak of multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae sepsis amongst neonates at a rural hospital in The Gambia, West Africa, involving 57 cases and case fatality of 60%. Here we undertook a retrospective pathogen genomic epidemiology study of clinical and environmental K. pneumoniae isolated during the outbreak, to identify the outbreak strain, refine the epidemic curve, confirm the environmental sources of contamination, monitor control of the outbreak, and characterise the outbreak strain in the context of the local and global pathogen population. Methods and Findings We sequenced all blood culture isolates identified as K. pneumoniae from patients aged 0–59 months (n=51 available, 77% from neonates), together with K. pneumoniae cultured from environmental samples during the outbreak investigation (n=16), and 56 stored blood culture surveillance isolates available from the previous decade (34 from neonates). Sequencing was performed using Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) Mk10 flowcells and a PromethION instrument, yielding mostly complete genomes (79%). Genomic analysis revealed 23% of isolates were K. quasipneumoniae and identified the outbreak strain as K. pneumoniae ST39 with capsular (K) locus KL62. This strain was responsible for 29 cases (16 fatalities) and was identified in three samples of intravenous fluids collected from the neonatal ward during the investigation. It harboured a ∼187 kbp IncF plasmid carrying the extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) gene bla CTX-M-15 and aac (3)- IId , encoding resistance to third-generation cephalosporins and gentamicin, respectively. The outbreak strain was not identified amongst historical surveillance isolates, and it was distinct from a KL23-ST39 strain responsible for an earlier outbreak at the Sir Edward Francis Small Teaching Hospital in Banjul, the country’s capital 7 years prior. Comparing the outbreak strain with publicly available genome data for ST39 and its associated sublineage (SL) 39, we observed SL39 has diversified into three common clonal groups, each associated with multiple K types, that have spread across Africa, Asia and Europe and have been associated with outbreaks of neonatal sepsis in Africa and elsewhere. We find SL39 is typically multidrug resistant, however the specific ESBL and carbapenemase genes vary by geographic location. Conclusions Pathogen whole-genome sequencing refined our understanding of the outbreak, allowing more precise identification to refine case numbers and case fatality calculations, and for precise identification of multi-use intravenous fluid bags as the source of the outbreak despite other samples being culture-positive for unrelated K. pneumoniae . This highlights the importance of infection prevention and control in reducing neonatal fatalities in low-resource settings, and the critical risk associated with multi-use reagents and equipment when caring for vulnerable neonates. The genomic analysis enabled us to identify and characterise the outbreak strain at high resolution, and together with global data highlights SL39 as an emerging high-risk multidrug-resistant, globally distributed clone of K. pneumoniae, capable of sustained transmission and high fatality. Impact Statement Neonatal sepsis caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae kills an estimated 800,000 infants annually, with the greatest burden in sub-Saharan Africa where multidrug-resistant strains are increasingly prevalent. Yet genomic investigations of outbreak strains from rural African settings remain scarce, limiting our understanding of transmission dynamics and the global emergence of high-risk lineages. In this study, we apply whole-genome sequencing to a multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae ST39 neonatal sepsis outbreak at a rural Gambian hospital, demonstrating how pathogen genomics can decisively refine outbreak investigations in low-resource settings: it corrected case counts, pinpointed contaminated multi-use intravenous fluid bags as the primary source, and revealed a novel ISKpn14-mediated chromosomal resistance island. Contextualising the outbreak strain within a global collection of 684 ST39 genomes, we identify sublineage 39 as a diversified, globally distributed, multidrug-resistant clone whose three dominant clonal groups have caused neonatal sepsis outbreaks across Africa, Asia, and Europe. Our findings reinforce the urgent need for sustained investment in genomic surveillance and infection prevention infrastructure in African neonatal units, and provide actionable data to guide targeted screening and vaccine design against prevalent African K. pneumoniae lineages. Data summary The raw sequencing data generated for this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) under BioProject accession PRJNA1367967. Individual isolate sequencing data are provided in Supplementary File 3 and are available under BioSample accessions SAMN53359187 through SAMN53359276, with corresponding SRA accessions SRR36200451 through SRR36200540. The complete genome assembly for a representative ST39 outbreak isolate, 38833B1 is available in GenBank under BioSample accession SAMN53359242, including the complete sequence of pNS39_A under GenBank accession PX620516 . Code used to generate the figures and reproduce the analyses presented in this study is available at https://github.com/efosternyarko/molecular-characterisation-klebsiella-pneumoniae-neonatal-sepsis-outbreak-gambia .

items.title: Spinal infection by Enterobacter hormaechei: an unusual cause of spondylodiscitis: a case report.
items.summary: INTRODUCTION: Spondylodiscitis is an infectious condition involving the intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies. Although Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are the most common pathogens, cases caused by Gram-negative bacilli are relatively rare. Enterobacter hormaechei is an exceptionally uncommon etiologic agent in this context. CASE PRESENTATION: A 69-year-old…

research.abstract: Abstract Introduction Spondylodiscitis is an infectious condition involving the intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies. Although Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are the most common pathogens, cases caused by Gram-negative bacilli are relatively rare. Enterobacter hormaechei is an exceptionally uncommon etiologic agent in this context. Case presentation A 69-year-old Turkish male with type 2 diabetes mellitus and a history of prostate adenocarcinoma in remission, with no active immunosuppression, presented with lower back pain and elevated inflammatory markers. Initially suspected to have metastatic spinal involvement, spinal MRI revealed spondylodiscitis at the T12–L1 level. Microbiological evaluation of the needle biopsy specimen yielded Enterobacter hormaechei . Species-level identification was established by culture and MALDI-TOF MS, with off-label syndromic PCR testing (BIOFIRE ® Joint Infection Panel) providing supportive concordant results. The patient was successfully managed with surgical intervention and appropriate antimicrobial therapy. Discussion Spondylodiscitis due to Enterobacter hormaechei remains exceedingly rare. This case highlights the importance of considering atypical Gram-negative organisms in spinal infections and underscores the value of advanced microbiological methods for accurate species-level identification.

items.title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
items.summary: PurposeTo compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). DesignRetrospective benchmarking study. Subjects4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

items.title: Circulating miR-26b-5p as a Potential Host-Derived Biomarker for Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis.
items.summary: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global infectious disease, and novel host-derived biomarkers are needed to improve diagnosis. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) are promising biomarkers due to their stability and immune regulatory functions; however, clinically validated TB-associated miRNAs remain limited. This study aimed to identify circulating miRNAs associated with active pulmonary…

research.abstract: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global infectious disease, and novel host-derived biomarkers are needed to improve diagnosis. Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) are promising biomarkers due to their stability and immune regulatory functions; however, clinically validated TB-associated miRNAs remain limited. This study aimed to identify circulating miRNAs associated with active pulmonary TB. Methods This study included 90 participants: active pulmonary TB (n=30), cured TB (n=30), and healthy controls (n=30). Candidate miRNAs were screened by pooled plasma miRNA profiling and further examined using three publicly available miRNA datasets. Circulating miR-26b-5p was quantified by RT-qPCR. Associations with active TB status were assessed using logistic regression, and discriminatory performance was evaluated by ROC analysis. Putative miR-26b-5p target genes and enriched pathways were explored using bioinformatic analyses. Results Microarray screening identified 108 candidate miRNAs, and cross-dataset analysis identified miR-26b-5p as the only overlapping candidate with consistent downregulation. Circulating miR-26b-5p was lower in active TB and higher in the clinically cured group. It remained associated with active-TB status after adjustment for BMI and PLR. miR-26b-5p showed an AUC of 0.867, while the combined model achieved an AUC of 0.956. Bioinformatic analysis identified 74 putative genes, with EP300, GSK3B, and PTEN as network hubs and PI3K-Akt among the enriched pathways. Conclusion Circulating miR-26b-5p was associated with active pulmonary TB and showed preliminary discriminatory value, supporting its further evaluation as a candidate host-response marker.

items.title: Natural selection on synonymous genetic variation in the major histocompatibility complex
items.summary: Protein coding DNA sequences harbor synonymous nucleotide variation that does not change amino acid sequences but influences phenotypes via multiple effects on the pathway from gene to protein. Synonymous variation has recently been shown to coevolve between viruses and their natural hosts, but its potential role in host immune defenses has not been explored. Here, I present evidence of natural…

research.abstract: Abstract Protein coding DNA sequences harbor synonymous nucleotide variation that does not change amino acid sequences but influences phenotypes via multiple effects on the pathway from gene to protein. Synonymous variation has recently been shown to coevolve between viruses and their natural hosts, but its potential role in host immune defenses has not been explored. Here, I present evidence of natural selection on synonymous variation in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), a highly polymorphic multigene locus that plays a crucial role in pathogen recognition by the adaptive immune system of vertebrate species. Using data from a wild population of Great Reed Warblers, I show that codon usage in exon 3 of MHC class I (MHC-I) genes is under strong purifying selection in 57 out of 87 codon sites. Scanning the Great Reed Warbler genome for tRNA genes revealed that, for most amino acids, bias towards preferred codons was associated with abundances of tRNA isotypes, indicating that the purifying selection is likely driven by selection for increased translational efficiency. However, spikes of synonymous variation appeared in 30 of the 87 sites in the MHC-I exon 3, and in those sites, codon usage bias and correlations with tRNA abundances were reduced. About half of these sites fall in CpG contexts, where cytosine deamination elevates the mutation rate; the other half do not, leaving the driver of much of the variation unexplained. The distribution of the spikes of synonymous variation showed no consistent association with structural domains of the MHC-I protein, nor with sites under positive selection for amino acid change, which are considered important for antigen binding properties. Intriguingly, the amount of synonymous variation in genotypes showed a positive correlation with Darwinian fitness, indicating that important evolutionary forces are at play that neutralize purifying selection in the 30 sites. From an ultimate perspective, the release of purifying selection among certain sites in MHC genes may indicate an arms race with pathogens, and I propose that the spikes of synonymous variation reveal a footprint of natural selection to escape inhibitory molecular interactions targeting MHC mRNA. I advance this RNA-level arms race as a novel axis of host–pathogen coevolution and a hypothesis to be tested directly. The fitness association is specific to synonymous variation, independent of amino-acid differences and the number of MHC alleles in genotypes, implicating selection on the synonymous variation itself rather than linked protein-level diversity. These results expose a previously unrecognized layer of selection in a key immune gene family and highlight the potential functional importance of synonymous variation in host–pathogen coevolution with direct implications for understanding susceptibility to infectious diseases. Significance Statement Roughly a quarter of DNA mutations carry no amino acid change, yet a growing body of evidence shows such synonymous variation can still shape how genes work. This study shows that genes of the major histocompatibility complex, central to how vertebrates detect infection, carry a hidden layer of natural selection acting on this synonymous variation, and that it is linked to individual fitness in a wild bird population. The findings suggest hosts and pathogens may be locked in an evolutionary arms race playing out beneath the level of protein sequence, with implications for how susceptibility to infectious disease is understood and studied.

items.title: Genomic characterization and evolutionary path of human satellite 1B in primates highlight a dynamic relationship with transposable elements
items.summary: Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ~2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). Here, we present the first comprehensive…

research.abstract: Abstract Human Satellite 1B (HSat1B) remains one of the least characterized classical human satellite DNAs, despite its massive abundance on the human Y chromosome. Its tripartite ∼2.5 kb monomer - comprising an AluY fragment, a GC-rich unit (here named H1B) and an AT-rich block - points to an evolutionary origin tightly linked to transposable elements (TEs). Here, we present the first comprehensive comparative genomic, phylogenetic, and transcriptional characterization of HSat1B across 10 primate species using Telomere-to-Telomere (T2T) and chromosome-scale long-read assemblies, combined with DNA-FISH, RNA-FISH and long-read transcriptomic analyses. We demonstrate that while canonical tandem HSat1B arrays are restricted to Homininae (human, chimpanzee, bonobo, and gorilla), the core H1B unit and its structural variants (H1Bsv1 and H1Bsv2) occur across all 10 primate genomes, including strepsirrhines (lemur). This indicates that the H1B sequence predates the assembly of the composite HSat1B monomer by at least 60 million years. H1B variants consistently map within TE-rich genomic contexts, supporting a stepwise, TE-mediated model of satellite diversification and mobilization. Within Homininae, humans exhibit a dramatic lineage-specific expansion driven by Yq12 amplification (∼14.2 Mb; 92% of total genomic content), whereas non-human great apes carry smaller, highly polymorphic autosomal and Y-linked arrays. Finally, we show that H1B-containing sequences are transcriptionally active in human and gorilla nuclei via RNA-FISH and characterize heterogeneous H1B/ Alu chimeric non-coding transcripts in the human male germline. Collectively, our findings uncover the birth and Homininae-specific expansion of a composite satellite DNA seeded by an ancient primate sequence module and sculpted by transposable elements.

items.title: Earl Grey ParTEA: scalable, consistent transposable element annotation from pangenomes to deep phylogenetic scopes
items.summary: Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent…

research.abstract: Abstract Transposable elements (TEs) are major drivers of genomic diversity, yet understanding their mobility and functional impact requires their accurate description in genomes. TE annotation is still typically performed genome-by-genome. TEs are often shared between some members of the same or closely related species. Hence, TE annotation with a library from a single reference misses families absent from that assembly, whereas building independent per-genome libraries fails to consistently surface shared TEs, hindering comparison. Here, we present Earl Grey ParTEA, a fully automated Snakemake pipeline extending the functionality of Earl Grey for comparative TE annotation across genome panels. ParTEA builds a single non-redundant TE library from all input genomes, resolves chimeric consensus sequences, and uses this shared library to annotate every genome, enabling direct comparison of TE family diversity, abundance, shared and private content, and activity landscapes. Optional modules provide TE library saturation analysis, BUSCO-based assembly quality control, and phylogenetic ordering of outputs. We applied ParTEA to sets of genomes spanning evolutionary scales: ten Arabidopsis thaliana accessions, ten Drosophila species, and ten species spanning the fungal kingdom. The Drosophila TE library expanded from 343 to 1,852 curated families including a previously missed rolling circle element with over 6,000 copies in D. miranda . The proportion of TE families shared across all genomes was highest within A. thaliana (97.3%), 37.7% across Drosophila species and only 0.5% across the set of fungi. ParTEA is available through Bioconda and represents a computationally efficient reproducible framework for comparative TE analysis in the era of large-scale genome analyses.

items.title: HiSpoT: a novel one-tube dual-barcode PCR method for NGS spoligotyping amplicon library preparation in Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex
items.summary: Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Tuberculosis remains one of the leading infectious causes of death globally, making rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing essential for effective outbreak tracking and epidemiological surveillance. To address the limitations and high costs of current typing methods, we developed a novel one-tube, dual-barcode PCR method for preparing targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) amplicon libraries for spoligotyping of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC), which we termed HiSpoT (High-throughput Spoligotyping by Targeted next generation sequencing). The assay targets 43 conserved spacer oligonucleotides in the CRISPR direct repeat (DR) region and is presented here together with the previously unpublished, difficult-to-design dual-barcode primer set needed to multiplex 96 samples in a single tube. HiSpoT is accurate, fast, high-throughput, and low-cost, eliminating the need for a commercial NGS library preparation kit. Because HiSpoT is PCR-based, the resulting spoligotypes remain directly comparable with the large PCR-based spoligotype databases accumulated over decades, enabling rapid outbreak tracking and biogeographic characterization of a country’s tuberculosis burden while higher-resolution whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data are obtained. Analysis of 288 clinical MTBC isolates from Israel (2020-2022) demonstrated a broad range of genetic lineages, and comparison of 79 isolates analyzed by both HiSpoT and WGS showed 70% full concordance, with essentially all discrepancies attributable to single-spacer insertion-element disruptions of PCR primer sites. We also present two open-source Google Colab Python tools, Spoligotyping_MTBC_gcl and its condensed HiSpoT_Spoligotyping_v8_ready VIBE variant, freely available on GitHub, which automatically process Illumina paired-end fastq output from HiSpoT or WGS and report binary and octal spoligotypes, spoligo international types (SIT), and MTBC family assignments with accompanying quality-control reports. IMPORTANCE Tuberculosis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis , is the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide, and rapid, accurate, and affordable strain typing is essential for tracking outbreaks and directing limited public health resources. The decades-old laboratory method for spoligotyping, a widely used genetic fingerprint for this bacterium, is slow, labor-intensive, and hard to read. Newer sequencing-based approaches solve these problems but usually still need an expensive, time-consuming commercial kit to prepare samples for sequencing. This work describes HiSpoT, a simplified, low-cost, one-tube method that prepares samples for sequencing without a commercial kit, cutting turnaround from about a week to about two days while testing many samples together. Because HiSpoT results agree with results obtained from older typing methods, laboratories anywhere with basic sequencing equipment can compare results to decades of stored international data. Two free, open-source computer programs are also provided so laboratories with limited bioinformatics expertise can analyze their sequencing data automatically.

items.title: Do divergent mitochondrial backgrounds alter the fate of nuclear alleles during hybridization and admixture?
items.summary: Hybridization brings together genetic variation from different populations or species into admixed genomes. As selection sorts this variation, the fate of each allele is determined by its fitness effect in the new hybrid genomic background. Because mitochondrial genes coevolve with the nuclear genome, they may be especially sensitive to foreign nuclear backgrounds, making them potential…

research.abstract: Abstract Hybridization brings together genetic variation from different populations or species into admixed genomes. As selection sorts this variation, the fate of each allele is determined by its fitness effect in the new hybrid genomic background. Because mitochondrial genes coevolve with the nuclear genome, they may be especially sensitive to foreign nuclear backgrounds, making them potential “hot-spots” for hybrid incompatibilities. Here, we test whether selection against mitonuclear incompatibilities drives repeatable hybridization outcomes. Specifically, we experimentally evolved three sets of five populations of hybrid Drosophila melanogaster , each carrying the same nuclear chromosomes but paired with one of three increasingly divergent mitochondrial DNA backgrounds. We hypothesized that accumulated incompatibilities would result in different patterns of nuclear admixture among mitochondrial backgrounds. To test this, we tracked nuclear allele frequencies in all 15 populations by whole-genome sequencing at intermediate time points. After 25 generations, we observed that rapid genomic evolution produced a strikingly parallel mosaic of both nuclear ancestries, independent of mitochondrial background. Contrary to our hypothesis, we found no evidence that mitochondrial background shaped nuclear admixture, even for interspecific combinations. These results suggest that in species with large effective population sizes, efficient purifying selection limits the accumulation of mitonuclear incompatibilities, allowing selection on nuclear alleles to promote repeatable ancestry sorting immediately following hybridization.

items.title: Retinopathy is more common, but age-related macular degeneration carries more visual impairment: a cross-sectional study of US adults graded from the same fundus photographs
items.summary: BackgroundRetinopathy and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are the most common findings on fundus photographs of older adults, yet their frequency, correlates and visual consequences have been estimated in separate samples. We compared them in a national survey that graded both from the same images. MethodsWe analyzed 5593 adults aged [≥]40 years in the US National Health and Nutrition…

research.abstract: Abstract Background Retinopathy and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) are the most common findings on fundus photographs of older adults, yet their frequency, correlates and visual consequences have been estimated in separate samples. We compared them in a national survey that graded both from the same images. Methods We analyzed 5593 adults aged ≥40 years in the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2005–2008 with photographs gradable for both conditions. We estimated survey-weighted prevalence, fitted identically specified logistic models for retinopathy (participants with diabetes) and AMD (full sample), and compared presenting visual impairment (better-eye acuity worse than 20/40) and self-rated vision across four groups: neither condition, retinopathy only, AMD only, and both. Results Retinopathy was more prevalent than AMD (9.54% [95% confidence interval (CI) 8.52–10.56] vs 6.52% [5.54–7.50]); AMD overtook it only from age 70 years. In participants with diabetes, retinopathy was associated with HbA1c (odds ratio [OR] 1.54 per percentage point; 1.33–1.78) and male sex (1.54; 1.10–2.17). AMD was associated with age (OR 1.09 per year; 1.07–1.11) and was less common in non-Hispanic Black adults (0.48; 0.33–0.71). Presenting impairment affected 4.91% of participants with neither condition, 7.09% with retinopathy only, 14.57% with AMD only and 26.15% with both. After age adjustment, impairment remained associated with AMD only (OR 2.23; 1.54–3.23) and both conditions (4.09; 2.28–7.37) but not retinopathy only (1.32; 0.91–1.90). Neither retinopathy nor diabetes was associated with AMD. Self-rated vision agreed poorly with measured impairment (κ = 0.15): only 12% of impaired participants rated their vision poor or very poor. Conclusions Retinopathy is the more frequent retinal finding in US adults aged ≥40 years, but AMD carries more of the measured visual impairment, independently of age. Grading diabetic screening photographs for AMD, and measuring acuity rather than asking about vision, would reach more people who see poorly.

items.title: Streamlined Point-of-Care Ultrasound Examination for Pulmonary Tuberculosis
items.summary: BackgroundPoint-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is a low-cost, radiation-free triage tool but lacks standardized acquisition protocols for tuberculosis (TB). We developed and evaluated a streamlined symmetric POCUS protocol for pulmonary TB in a high-burden setting. MethodsUgandan participants aged [≥]13 years with confirmed pulmonary TB, household TB exposure, or a non-TB respiratory condition…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is a low-cost, radiation-free triage tool but lacks standardized acquisition protocols for tuberculosis (TB). We developed and evaluated a streamlined symmetric POCUS protocol for pulmonary TB in a high-burden setting. Methods Ugandan participants aged ≥13 years with confirmed pulmonary TB, household TB exposure, or a non-TB respiratory condition underwent an 18-position POCUS examination (12 lung zones and 6 pre-established extrapulmonary positions). Random Forest classifiers using prespecified pathologic features were developed in a fixed stratified 75/25 training/holdout split. All symmetric 2-, 4-, and 6-zone combinations were evaluated in training data. The best protocol of each size was locked and tested in the holdout set. Results Among 318 analyzed participants, 118 (37.1%) had pulmonary TB and 200 were TB-negative, including 102 with other respiratory conditions (ORC). The model-selected 6-zone protocol comprised bilateral anterior-superior, lateral-superior, and posterior-superior lung zones. For TB versus all TB-negative participants, the AUCs for the 6-zone, 12-zone, and 18-position protocols were 0.82 (95% CI, 0.73-0.92), 0.81 (0.70–0.92), and 0.81 (0.71–0.91), respectively (all P > 0.76). For TB versus ORC, AUCs were 0.81 (0.70–0.91), 0.85 (0.76–0.93), and 0.85 (0.76–0.94), respectively (all P > 0.45). The 2-zone protocol had a lower AUC than the 6-zone protocol for TB versus all TB-negative participants ( P = 0.004). Shred sign, consolidation, and B-lines with irregular pleura were the strongest TB-associated findings. Conclusions A fixed 6-zone lung POCUS examination showed similar discrimination for TB to more comprehensive 12-lung-zone and 18-position protocols. This supports a simpler, scalable approach to TB triage.

items.title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
items.summary: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36…

research.abstract: Abstract Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analysed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4⁺ T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5 . Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

items.title: Decision for hysterectomy as a modifiable cardiovascular risk factor: A systematic review and meta-analysis
items.summary: ObjectiveTo describe the role of hysterectomy in modifying the major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Data sourcesPubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ScienceDirect were searched from database inception to March 10, 2026. Study eligibility criteriaFull-text randomized controlled trials, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, case series, and…

research.abstract: Abstract Objective To describe the role of hysterectomy in modifying the major atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Data sources PubMed, Cochrane Library, Embase, and ScienceDirect were searched from database inception to March 10, 2026. Study eligibility criteria Full-text randomized controlled trials, case-control studies, cross-sectional studies, cohort studies, case series, and experimental studies reporting new-onset cardiovascular events, diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, or other metabolic effects following hysterectomy were eligible. Reviews and book chapters were excluded. Study appraisal and synthesis methods Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by multiple reviewers with conflicts resolved by consensus. Cohort study quality was assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale; a modified version assessed cross-sectional studies. Meta-analyses were performed using a generic inverse-variance random-effects model for each outcome, stratified by study design (cross-sectional versus cohort) and effect measure (adjusted odds ratio, adjusted hazard ratio, or relative risk). Narrative synthesis was performed for outcomes not meeting criteria for meta-analysis. Results Twenty studies (11 cohort, 8 cross-sectional, 1 mixed design) were included after screening 18,337 records from four databases. Hysterectomy was associated with significantly increased risk of hypertension (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.32, 95% confidence interval 1.18– 1.48; cohort hazard ratio 1.19, 95% confidence interval 1.09–1.30), diabetes (cross-sectional odds ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.11–1.32; cohort hazard ratio 1.20, 95% confidence interval 1.13–1.29), hyperlipidemia (hazard ratio 1.21, 95% confidence interval 1.13–1.29), obesity (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.03–1.50), and metabolic syndrome (odds ratio 1.24, 95% confidence interval 1.08–1.44). Conclusions Hysterectomy is associated with increased risk of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and metabolic syndrome, key modifiable atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk factors. Active cardiovascular risk assessment and follow-up may be warranted for women who undergo hysterectomy, particularly at a young age.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Misinformation decreases public confidence in health technologies and willingness to use them. Psychological inoculation, or “prebunking”, exposes people to misleading claims before they spread widely and refutes the claims and embedded persuasion tactics. Evidence on its effectiveness for HIV-related misinformation, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and among young women (a population highly vulnerable to HIV), is limited. Methods We conducted a randomised controlled trial (July to October 2025) among 2,163 women aged 18-29 years recruited online in South Africa. Participants were randomly assigned to view two short TikTok-style inoculation videos addressing common myths about an HIV vaccine, or attention-matched control videos on nutrition and diabetes. All participants then viewed multiple false claims presented as social media posts. The primary outcome was intention to receive an HIV vaccine if available (1-10 scale), assessed immediately post-intervention and at three-week follow-up. Secondary outcomes included likelihood of recommending the vaccine; and perceived credibility, emotional impact, and shareability of misinformation claims. We used linear regression models to estimate intervention effects. Results Misinformation exposure reduced vaccine intentions by 0.63 points in the control group, while intentions increased by 0.30 points in the intervention group. Controlling for covariates and baseline intentions, post-exposure vaccine intentions were 0.92 points higher in the intervention group (95% CI 0.78, 1.06; p<0.01), a 12% relative increase. Intervention participants were also more likely to recommend the vaccine (+0.74; 95% CI 0.61, 0.88; p<0.01). Inoculation reduced perceived credibility, emotional distress, and sharing intentions across all false claims. Effects persisted at three-week follow-up (vaccine intentions: +0.97; 95% CI 0.78, 1.17; p<0.01). Conclusion Brief, scalable psychological inoculation delivered via social-media-style videos protected young women’s HIV vaccine intentions, with effects generalising to novel claims and persisting over three weeks. Prebunking campaigns may safeguard public confidence in other new HIV prevention technologies like lenacapavir.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Cultivated peanut ( Arachis hypogaea L.) is an allotetraploid crop (2n = 4x = 40) with an AABB genome that preserves extensive synteny between its two subgenomes. This characteristic, along with the availability of multiple genomic resources, provides a valuable framework for the comprehensive characterization of gene families and for inferring their evolutionary dynamics. Here we report a genome-wide analysis of the Dof transcription factor family in peanut (AhyDof), including phylogenetic inferences, gene structures, chromosomal locations, patterns of gene duplication, and expression analysis. Results ​A total of 66 non-redundant Dof genes (AhyDofs) were identified and unevenly distributed across the A and B subgenom​es. Comparative analyses revealed extensive conservation of gene structure, protein motifs, and chromosomal localization among homeologous genes inherited from the diploid progenitors, indicating that allopolyploidization contributed to family expansion while having a limited impact on gene diversification. Phylogenetic analyses placed AhyDofs within the four major angiosperm Dof lineages, supporting the evolutionary conservation of this family across flowering plants. Synteny analyses further identified chromosomal rearrangements and tandem duplication events contributing to the current composition of the AhyDof repertoire. Most notably, we discovered a novel group of six Dof genes associated with previously undescribed Pack-MULE transposons, designated AMuD, providing the first evidence of Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication in the genus Arachis . Structural and phylogenetic analyses suggested that these elements originated from non-autonomous MULEs and captured an ancestral Dof gene related to AhyDof-15.3. The dN/dS rate analysis suggested that transduplicated genes may have evolved under selective constraint, potentially indicating that functional constraints were maintained after mobilization. Comparative genomic analyses, PCR assays across diploid species, and Oxford Nanopore sequencing data suggested that AMuD elements originated within the B–F–K lineage of section Arachis and were maintained during peanut domestication and diversification. Promoter analyses revealed distinct cis-regulatory architectures among AMuD-derived genes, while transcriptomic data demonstrated their transcriptional activity, particularly in reproductive tissues. Conclusions The evolution of the peanut Dof repertoire in peanut was shaped by multiple mechanisms, including polyploidization, chromosomal rearrangements, tandem duplication, and lineage-specific Pack-MULE-mediated transduplication. The discovery of AMuD elements reveals a previously undescribed mechanism contributing to the diversification of regulatory genes in Arachis and provides new insights into the evolutionary dynamics of plant transcription factor families.

items.summary: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. We also provide new hardware implementations…

research.abstract: Efficient evaluation of sequence data likelihoods and their high-dimensional gradients on phylogenetic trees improves inference under both maximum-likelihood and Bayesian frameworks. Here, we present BEAGLE 4.1, a high-performance library for statistical phylogenetics that incorporates new algorithms to evaluate these gradients on phylogenetic trees. We also provide new hardware implementations for both likelihoods and gradients supporting ARM NEON intrinsics and optimized matrix multiplication units -- called tensor cores -- on NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs). We benchmark the performance scaling of the library across a number of patterns and taxa on multi-core CPUs and GPUs, and compare the speedup afforded by NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as well as performance scaling with an increasing number of GPUs. We show that multi-core CPU implementations provide up to a fourfold speedup over single-threaded CPU implementations and up to an tenfold speedup for nucleotide and codon models, respectively, with performance generally improving as the number of taxa and site patterns increases. GPUs outperform multi-threaded CPU implementations for a realistic number of patterns, even for nucleotide models with a small state-space size of 4, while for codon models they provide substantially higher performance gains even for a single pattern or four taxa. Tensor cores on GPUs provide up to 2-fold speedup relative to standard CUDA cores for codon models. Using NEON instructions on ARM CPUs affords up to a $\sim 1.3$-fold speedup over non-SIMD implementation with the speedup going down to 1.1-fold at 8 CPU threads. We provide these new algorithms to evaluate the gradient and efficient hardware implementations for both likelihood and gradient calculations through BEAGLE 4.1, such that they can be readily integrated into phylogenetic software packages.

research.abstract: Abstract Background Identifying functional variants that influence human health remains a challenge in human genetics. Conventional genotype-phenotype association studies test millions of variants, imposing a substantial multiple-testing burden as genomic and biobank datasets expand in size and variant diversity. Additionally, the contribution of structural variation, which is a substantial driver of genetic diversity, remains underexplored in these studies. Signatures of recent positive selection offer a powerful biological basis for prioritizing potentially functional variation, although demographic history can confound their detection and interpretation in these analyses. Results We performed evolution-guided association mapping using long-read genomes from 1,027 self-identified Black or African American participants in the All of Us Research Program and short-read genomes from an additional 38,552 matched participants of African-ancestry. Using demography-calibrated inferences, we identified 228 genomic regions with local ancestry enrichment or depletion and 1,616 candidate loci showing putative recent positive selection signals. These loci were enriched for genic and regulatory sequences, as well as previously reported eQTL, sQTL, and GWAS associations. Leveraging the resolution of the long-read data, we mapped 15 structural variants to these candidate loci, including 10 located within 1,000 base pairs of putative cis -regulatory enhancers. Admixture- and selection-based phenome-wide association testing identified 13 and 446 nominal associations, respectively, 17 of which remained significant following replication and meta-analysis. Conclusions Our results support the use of evolutionary signatures as a robust framework for uncovering clinically relevant variation, including structural variants, in underrepresented populations.

research.abstract: In 2023, an estimated 13% of worldwide deaths resulting from antimicrobial resistance (AMR) were due to drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). The World Health Organization (WHO) documented a dramatic, sixfold increase in the number of patients treated with 6-month all-oral (BPaLM) regimens, from 5,653 patients in 2023, to 34,000 patients by 2024, while also documenting an emergence of bedaquiline resistance in real-world cohorts and a lack of efficacy of BCG revaccination in the BCG-PRIME Phase 2b trial against sustained Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Concurrently, the M72/AS01E subunit vaccine trial completed recruitment (approximately 20,000 individuals) across five high-burden countries, 11 months ahead of scheduled completion date. The first randomized controlled trial assessing DRTB-HDT host-directed therapy for DR-TB in adults (metformin + dovramilast), conducted at five international sites, is entering the late-stage readout phase. This synthesis of data, covering the period from 2015 through 2026, across six different dimensions includes molecular mechanisms of resistance, novel antimicrobial treatment modalities, host-directed therapy, immunity associated with regulatory compliance, adjuvants to vaccines, and the clinical translation of vaccine candidates. The Molecular-to-Translational continuum is used as a framework for the synthesis, with the regulatory immune function domain (T regulatory cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, and check-point axes) linking all five domains. Our central hypothesis is that drug resistance evolution of the microbe and failure of the host to maintain regulatory immunity are interdependent and create a bidirectional relationship with each other. We have identified nine major research gaps, with milestone dates from 2026 to 2030, based on unresolved controversies regarding the bedaquiline resistance catalog and the acquisition versus transmission narrative.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Active case finding (ACF) in India screens large populations to find few cases. AI-NETRA predicts neighbourhood-level tuberculosis (TB) risk from routine notification data and generates field microplans. OBJECTIVE: To compare the yield and efficiency of AI-guided and standard ACF, and frontline acceptability. DESIGN: Prospective quasi-experimental evaluation in four TB Units of Pune district, comparing two-week AI-guided sweeps (April to May 2026) with the routine campaign in the same units (December 2024 to January 2025). Primary endpoint: bacteriologically confirmed pulmonary TB per persons screened; secondary: all-forms yield, presumptive yield, referral precision, number needed to screen (NNS) and cost per case. Acceptability: 16 focus groups (n=100) and a survey of 101 ASHAs. RESULTS: AI-guided teams screened 66,095 people and confirmed 10 pulmonary cases, against 9 among 177,322 in the standard campaign (rate ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.09 to 8.29); NNS was 6,610 versus 19,702 and cost per case 66% lower. All-forms detection did not differ (15 versus 32; RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.39); the standard campaign had mobile X-ray. 96% of ASHAs reported finding the same presumptive cases while screening fewer people. CONCLUSION: Geospatial targeting raised confirmed yield per person and lowered NNS; total detection did not differ. A concurrent, like-for-like trial is warranted.

We applied an integrative multi-omics approach within a deeply phenotyped twin cohort to identify systemic molecular signatures and pathways associated with NDCs. Our study included 237 twins aged 8-28 years from the Roots of Autism and ADHD…

research.abstract: Abstract Neurodevelopmental conditions (NDCs) arise from complex genetic-environmental interactions, yet their molecular underpinnings remain incompletely defined. We applied an integrative multi-omics approach within a deeply phenotyped twin cohort to identify systemic molecular signatures and pathways associated with NDCs. Our study included 237 twins aged 8-28 years from the Roots of Autism and ADHD Twin Study in Sweden (RATSS), with one or more omics layers available per individual, including serum and cerebrospinal fluid proteomics, urine and fecal metabolomics, blood metallomics, and whole-genome sequencing in a subset of 14 monozygotic (MZ) twin pairs. Using the DIABLO framework, we identified cross-omics features that distinguish individuals with and without NDCs. The identified features converged on enriched metabolic and immune-related pathways, including purine metabolism, lysine degradation, PI3K-Akt, and MAPK signaling. Several key molecules also showed differential abundance at the single-molecule level in generalized estimating equation (GEE) models. ADA protein, pyrimidine-related metabolites (thymidine, glutamine, and 2’-deoxyuridine), and copper showed suggestive associations within NDC-discordant MZ twin pairs, pointing to potential non-shared condition-related effects, while flavin mononucleotide and manganese associations with NDCs were influenced by shared genetic or familial environmental factors. Our findings indicate that NDC-related molecular alterations manifest across multiple biological layers and tissues, and are detectable through integrative systems-level analysis. Our scalable framework provides critical insights into altered metabolic and immune processes in NDCs and highlights candidate features that may inform future biomarker development and mechanistic research in precision psychiatry.

research.abstract: 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across 64 species and 18 loci (L = 26,700 aligned columns; Lagomorpha outgroups, Sciuromorpha, Castorimorpha, Dipodoidea, invasive Muridae, and New World Cricetidae: Arvicolinae, Neotominae, and Sigmodontinae) coupled with 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three North American PopSets (Peromyscus maniculatus, Sigmodon hispidus, and Urocitellus parryii; 3 × N = 36 = 108 conspecific isolates) benchmarked against *MAFFT, *IQ-TREE/*LSD2, *PAML codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4 The continental radiation of rodents (Order Rodentia) across North America via Paleogene Beringian corridors, Miocene grassland expansions, and Great American Biotic Interchange exchanges—coupled with the Anthropocene introduction of Old World commensal murids—established both the foundational small-mammal trophic guilds of Nearctic ecosystems and the primary sylvatic reservoirs for North America's major rodent-borne zoonoses. Here we execute a 32-chain RuNIE phylogenomic and functional selection analysis across an 18-locus, 64-species Glires supermatrix (L = 26,700 aligned columns with 7,979 parsimony-informative sites and 8,803 distinct site patterns) paired with independent 10,000-generation (20% burn-in) single-species Bayesian coalescent skyline reconstructions across three conspecific North American population datasets (3 × N = 36 = 108 isolates) benchmarking Native Rust against *MAFFT v7.526, *IQ-TREE v2.4.0 with *LSD2 v2.4.4, *PAML v4.10.10 codeml, and *BEAST v1.10.4. Our fossil-calibrated chronogram anchors the Glires root (Lagomorpha vs. Rodentia) at 65.2 Ma, Crown Rodentia at 56.8 Ma, the Sciuromorpha–Castorimorpha split at 36.4 Ma, Myodonta (Dipodoidea vs. Muroidea) at 46.5 Ma, the Muridae–Cricetidae divergence at 24.8 Ma, Crown Cricetidae at 18.6 Ma, and the New World Neotominae–Sigmodontinae split at 13.4 Ma. Codon selection modeling (*PAML codeml) reveals strong purifying constraint on the Sin Nombre hantavirus endothelial receptor ITGB3 beta-3 integrin (omega = 0.5319), intermediate selective constraint on the high-altitude and fossorial hypoxia axis EPAS1/HBB (omega = 0.0343) and rodenticide-detoxification locus VKORC1/CYP2C (omega = 0.2572), and diversifying positive selection on bacterial pattern-recognition receptors TLR2/TLR4 (omega = 0.2631) and the New World Arenavirus receptor TFRC transferrin receptor 1 apical domain (omega = 0.1453). Across the three single-species PopSet skyline cohorts, we resolve post-glacial forest/oak-mast expansion and contemporary ENSO Sin Nombre hantavirus / Lyme disease amplification in the North American deer mouse (Peromyscus maniculatus, N = 36, Ne = 433,194 to 653,847; *BEAST = 667,970), northward agricultural grassland expansion and Black Creek Canal / Tamiami viral irruptions in the hispid cotton rat (Sigmodon hispidus, N = 36, Ne = 1,534,254 to 1,753,302; *BEAST = 1,808,005), and post-LGM Beringian steppe-tundra recolonization and high-latitude permafrost-thaw dynamics in the Arctic ground squirrel (Urocitellus parryii, N = 36, Ne = 707,606 to 1,687,680; *BEAST = 1,740,336), while demonstrating that Native Rust achieves a 42.9-fold end-to-end speedup (13.88 s vs. 595.24 s Hybrid and 1861.52 s full External UFBoot).
