research.journal: Cold Spring Harbor Perspectives in Medicine
research.abstract: Tuberculosis (TB), caused by infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), represents an important cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide for which an improved vaccine and immunodiagnostics are urgently needed. CD4+ and CD8+ T cells play an important role in host defense to TB. Definition of the immunodominant antigens recognized by these T cells is critical for improved understanding of the immunobiology of TB and for development of vaccines and diagnostics. Herein, we review antigens and epitopes recognized by classically human leukocyte antigen (HLA) class I- and class II-restricted CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in humans infected with MTB, as defined using either targeted or genome-wide approaches. We address the extent to which these antigens have been defined as immunodominant, protective, and/or specific to disease stages in humans and, with particular relevance to CD8+ T-cell recognition, whether these antigens are displayed by MTB-infected cells.

items.title: Lymphangiogenesis is Critical for Healing and Survival in a Murine Model of Laryngotracheal Injury
items.summary: Objective: Lymphatic dysfunction has been implicated in exacerbating fibrosis in numerous diseases, yet the role of the lymphatic system in laryngotracheal injury has not previously been explored. This study aims to evaluate lymphatic vascular remodeling in a murine model of laryngotracheal stenosis (LTS) and determine how pharmacologic blockade of lymphangiogenesis impacts airway healing after…

research.abstract: Abstract Objective Lymphatic dysfunction has been implicated in exacerbating fibrosis in numerous diseases, yet the role of the lymphatic system in laryngotracheal injury has not previously been explored. This study aims to evaluate lymphatic vascular remodeling in a murine model of laryngotracheal stenosis (LTS) and determine how pharmacologic blockade of lymphangiogenesis impacts airway healing after mucosal injury. Methods LTS was induced in C57BL6 mice using an established chemomechanical injury model. Lymphatic density was quantified using LYVE-1 immunohistochemistry. Mice were treated with the VEGFR-3-selective tyrosine kinase inhibitor SAR131675 to block lymphangiogenesis after injury. Outcomes assessed included survival, histopathology, immunohistochemistry, and Evans blue dye vascular leakage. Results Laryngotracheal injury induced a substaantial increase in subepithelial lymphatic vessel density concomitant with fibrotic remodeling. Pharmacologic inhibition of VEGFR-3 signaling with SAR131675 abrogated this lymphangiogenic response and resulted in markedly increased mortality, impaired epithelial repair with obstructive sloughing, increased edema, and persistent histopathologic evidence of tissue injury. A qualitative increase in pathologic fibrocellular remodeling was also observed, though with no measurable difference in lamina propria thickness. Conclusion These findings establish lymphatic remodeling as an essential component of successful airway repair following mucosal injury. Lymphatic dysfunction is a common feature of known risk factors for LTS including diabetes, obesity, and prematurity, and can be exacerbated by positive pressure ventilation. Disruption of the lymphangiogenic response to airway injury may lead to stasis of pro-inflammatory factors that result in chronic inflammation, maladaptive remodeling, and pathologic tissue changes. The lymphatic vasculature is a viable target for future mechanistic study and potential therapeutic intervention following airway injury.

items.title: Diet-Related Molecular Evolution Differs between Vertivores, Invertivores, and Combined Carnivores
items.summary: Mammals have repeatedly evolved specialized diets, including a variety of predatory diets targeting different prey animals. Prior research has found differences in positive selection, gene family evolution and gene functional loss linked with diet, but has focused primarily on trophic level classifications of herbivory, carnivory, and omnivory. Here we divide "carnivores" into vertivores and…

research.abstract: Abstract Mammals have repeatedly evolved specialized diets, including a variety of predatory diets targeting different prey animals. Prior research has found differences in positive selection, gene family evolution, and gene functional loss across diets, but has primarily classified mammals into the three categories of herbivory, carnivory, and omnivory. Here we divide “carnivores” into vertivores and invertivores, due to the differences in nutrient composition of those food sources. We find significant differences in molecular evolutionary rates of multiple genes and gene sets between vertivores and invertivores, with vertivores having lower evolutionary rates of immune related genes, and invertivores having lower evolutionary rates of DNA repair genes and olfactory genes. By comparing evolutionary rates of vertivores, invertivores, and the combination of all carnivores against herbivores, we find that the method of classifying predatory species influences findings of differences between predators and herbivores. Our results in the combined carnivore-herbivore comparison are more similar to those of the invertivore-herbivore comparison than to those of the vertivore-herbivore comparison, which suggests that prior studies on carnivory may have been detecting patterns of molecular evolution related to invertivory. Lineages across all predatory diets have lower evolutionary rates of lipid metabolism genes relative to herbivores, though the specific genes and pathways showing these signatures, particularly those related to steroid hormone metabolism, differ between predatory diets. Taken together, these analyses of molecular evolutionary rates across nuanced predatory diets provide novel insights into the evolution of vertebrate- and invertebrate-based diets, as well as carnivory as a whole. Significance Statement Several studies have used genome-wide gene sequences from mammals with different diets to identify genes with patterns of natural selection related to diet. However, these studies were limited in part due to the common choice to combine invertebrate-based (e.g., insects, shellfish) and vertebrate-based (e.g., fish, birds, other mammals) diets in their analyses. By separating these diets in our study, we identify genes that experienced selection related to these different food sources across mammals, and provide clarification of patterns found by previous studies.

items.title: Contrasting Range and Demographic Histories in two Palearctic Dragonfly Species (Odonata: Anisoptera)
items.summary: Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica, a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis, a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined…

research.abstract: ABSTRACT Climatic suitability is often used to infer historical range changes, yet whether suitable area predicts effective population size remains unexplored. We investigated this relationship in two Palearctic dragonflies with contrasting ecologies: Somatochlora arctica , a widespread peatland specialist, and S. meridionalis , a southern European species associated with shaded streams. We combined demographic reconstructions from individual reference genomes using the pairwise sequentially Markovian coalescent (PSMC), maximum entropy (MaxEnt) species distribution models projected across six paleoclimatic intervals spanning approximately 3.3 million years, and ancestral state reconstructions of peatland specialization. Predicted suitable area was consistently greater for S. arctica , reaching its greatest extent during the Last Glacial Maximum. However, its inferred effective population size was smaller than that of S. meridionalis for most of the last ∼275,000 years. Ancestral reconstructions placed the most probable gain of peatland specialization in the S. arctica lineage (Clade I) during the late Miocene, with a median age of 9.4 million years, predating the modeled climatic intervals. These findings indicate a decoupling of climatic suitability and demographic history. Patchy breeding habitat, population structure, and the isolated Scottish origin of the sampled S. arctica may contribute to this mismatch. Combining genomic, ecological, and phylogenetic approaches provides complementary insights into historical biogeography and highlights the limitations of interpreting suitable climate as available breeding habitat or using individual genomes to characterize species-wide demographic histories.

At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$…

research.abstract: Computing phylogenetic likelihoods becomes challenging when the continuous-time Markov chain has a large state space. At each branch, pruning algorithms require terms of the form $e^{Q t}\cdot B$, where $Q$ is an $S \times S$ rate matrix (e.g., for $S$ states), $t$ is a branch length, and the columns of matrix $B$ (e.g., $B \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{S \times L}$) are partial-likelihood vectors for $L$ site patterns. Many implementations calculate the dense transition matrix $P(t)=e^{Q t}$ via eigendecomposition and multiply it by $B$. This strategy is efficient for small state spaces, but it can be inefficient for large sparse rate matrices because forming $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices destroys sparsity and its cost may not be well amortized when $L$ is small. We implement an alternative likelihood kernel based on the Al-Mohy and Higham (2011) algorithm for computing the action of the matrix exponential directly, avoiding explicit construction of $P(t)$ or its eigen vector matrices. The resulting method takes full advantage of the sparsity of $Q$. We implement this method as a CPU-based extension to the BEAGLE library and evaluate it on two large-state molecular models: a Markov-modulated codon model of heterotachy with $M$ selective regimes and $61\cdot M$ possible states, and a codon-pair model of interlocus gene conversion between two paralogs with $61^2=3\,721$ possible states. Our results characterize when action-based likelihood computation improves performance over calculating $e^{Q t}$ directly. We show that this method enables fast, scalable inference for complex models, removing a key computational barrier to the study of evolution with large state space models.

items.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the Three-Gene Host-Response Test in Blood for Tuberculosis: A Systematic Review.
items.summary: Purpose Molecular diagnostic tests and sputum-based assays are common techniques for the initial evaluation of tuberculosis (TB). However, given their limitations in certain clinical contexts, efforts have been made to develop other diagnostic markers. This review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a three-gene host-response test (TB score) for the diagnosis of TB. Methods We performed…

research.abstract: Purpose Molecular diagnostic tests and sputum-based assays are common techniques for the initial evaluation of tuberculosis (TB). However, given their limitations in certain clinical contexts, efforts have been made to develop other diagnostic markers. This review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a three-gene host-response test (TB score) for the diagnosis of TB. Methods We performed systematic searches in seven databases until July 2026. We included observational studies evaluating the diagnostic accuracy of the TB score to diagnosis of TB across different clinical contexts. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2. Meta-analysis was performed using the logit function, and GRADE was employed to assess certainty of evidence (CoE). Results Twenty-eight studies were included. For distinguishing pulmonary TB from other respiratory diseases, the TB score showed a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.80 (95% CI: 0.73-0.84) and 0.72 (95% CI: 0.64-0.78), respectively, with an AUC of 0.82. When comparing pulmonary TB to healthy controls, sensitivity was 0.75 and specificity was 0.86, with an AUC of 0.87. Performance was lower for meningeal tuberculosis (sensitivity 0.58; specificity 0.67) and for distinguishing active from latent TB (sensitivity 0.73; specificity 0.76). Risk of bias was generally low. The CoE for most outcomes was very low. Conclusion The TB score shows moderate diagnostic accuracy for pulmonary TB, with pooled sensitivity below the WHO TPP minimum for a standalone triage test. High heterogeneity and very low CoE limit confidence in these findings. Its potential role as a complementary tool remains investigational and requires validation in prospective studies.

items.title: Polygenic overlap of physical activity with schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease
items.summary: Physical activity levels are increasingly investigated as candidate digital biomarkers across a range of psychiatric and neurological disorders. Physical activity is heritable, with associated genetic variants implicating genes expressed in the central nervous system. However, its shared genetic architecture with disorders such as schizophrenia and Parkinsons disease (PD) remains poorly…

research.abstract: Physical activity levels are increasingly investigated as candidate digital biomarkers across a range of psychiatric and neurological disorders. Physical activity is heritable, with associated genetic variants implicating genes expressed in the central nervous system. However, its shared genetic architecture with disorders such as schizophrenia and Parkinson's disease (PD) remains poorly understood. Here, we applied complementary genome-wide methods to investigate the genetic overlap between physical activity and these disorders. We used a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of objectively measured physical activity (n = 89,683), enhanced through multi-trait GWAS incorporating self-reported activity measures (n = 124,842-377,234). In cross-trait analysis with recent GWAS of schizophrenia (n = 53,386 cases, 77,258 controls) and PD (63,555 cases, 17,700 proxy cases, and 1,746,386 controls), we find that while genetic correlations are negligible (rg=-0.02-0.02, p>0.05), polygenic overlap was substantial, with the majority of trait-influencing variants shared between the three traits. This contrast reflects mixed effect directions, which we show through convergent results from causal mixture modelling, local genetic correlations, and conjunctional false discovery rate analysis. Genes shared between activity and schizophrenia were differentially expressed in the amygdala and several basal ganglia structures, and associated with a range of cognitive-affective traits. In contrast, genes shared between activity and PD were largely associated with neurodegenerative disorders and structural brain phenotypes. Together, these findings suggest that activity draws on genes involved in motor, cognitive, affective and neurodegenerative processes, providing a genetic basis for its alteration across diverse neuropsychiatric disorders.

research.abstract: ObjectivesPrecision oncology relies on accurate interpretation of tumour-detected gene variants, to guide personalised treatment decisions. However, interpretation of variants in context requires extensive information that is often buried within unstructured biomedical literature and obscured by inconsistent nomenclature, making manual retrieval labour-intensive and prone to omissions. In this study, our aim was to evaluate the potential of large language models to extract variant-treatment-cancer associations at scale from published abstracts. DesignWe developed Variantscape, a large-scale, automated pipeline and open-access web tool. It integrates traditional natural language processing methods with state-of-the-art large language models to extract, standardise, and analyse co-associations between genetic variants, cancer types, and therapeutic interventions from published biomedical abstracts. ResultsFrom over 3.7 million abstracts published between January 2014 and October 2026, 886,195 articles containing gene names were eligible for extraction. Among these, 37,895 (4.3%) mentioned a variant, cancer type, and therapeutic agent together, covering 11,985 unique variants across 197 cancer types and 547 therapeutic agents. LLM verification against the abstract text confirmed at least one association in 35,224 papers, giving a literature-derived graph of 10,571 nodes and 44,644 verified edges. Canonical alterations in well-studied cancers (e.g., BRAF V600E in melanoma) were strongly linked to established treatments, while several rare variants also emerged with high-confidence literature support. ConclusionsBy applying large language models to biomedical literature, Variantscape enables scalable, context-aware extraction of trilateral variant-treatment-cancer relationships. This approach supports early evidence synthesis/hypothesis generation, highlights underrecognized or rare associations for MTB preparation, and offers a practical resource for accelerating discovery and supporting precision oncology research and translation. FundingThis study was funded by the School of Medicine at the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland under grant number 2300380. Article SummaryO_ST_ABSStrengths and limitations of this studyC_ST_ABS[bullet] Variantscape combines traditional natural language processing with large language models to enable scalable, automated extraction of variant-cancer-treatment relationships from over 3.7 million biomedical abstracts, substantially reducing the manual search burden inherent to existing molecular tumour board workflows. [bullet]The pipeline applies large language model-based inference to standardise inconsistent genetic nomenclature across the literature, improving the comparability and reliability of extracted associations that would otherwise be obscured by terminological variation. [bullet]Variantscape is designed as a continuously updatable, open-access resource, meaning it can incorporate newly published evidence without requiring repeated manual intervention. [bullet]The pipeline relies solely on abstract-level text rather than full-text articles, which may limit the depth and granularity of extracted associations, as key methodological details, variant context, and nuanced clinical findings are frequently reported only within the body of published papers. [bullet]Automated extraction using large language models introduces a risk of misattribution of variant-cancer-treatment relationships, and without systematic manual validation of outputs, the precision of identified associations at scale remains difficult to fully characterise.

research.abstract: BACKGROUND: Species inhabiting high-elevation environments face energetic and physiological challenges, creating opportunities for adaptive divergence from lowland taxa. The yellow-tailed woolly monkey (Lagothrix flavicauda), a Critically Endangered primate endemic to high-elevation forests in Andean Perú, provides a unique system for investigating the evolutionary consequences of long-term occupation of high elevations. We used Oxford Nanopore Technology (ONT) to generate a high-coverage mitochondrial reference genome using low-quality fecal samples. Using this and a new mitogenome from a closely-related lowland common woolly monkey (L. lagotricha poeppigii), we estimated divergence dates and calculated substitution ratios to investigate the evolutionary history of both Lagothrix taxa and assess whether high-elevation living has left signatures of selection in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation genes of L. flavicauda. RESULTS: We assembled a high-coverage (9190X) reference mitogenome of 16,603 bp for L. flavicauda from a 15-year-old fecal sample, and a novel mitogenome for L. lagotricha poeppigii from fresh tissue (112X, 16,590 bp). Our phylogenetic reconstruction is consistent with other platyrrhine primate phylogenies with high bootstrap support, with the two Lagothrix taxa showing evidence of having diverged from one another ~ 2.8 million years ago. Substitution (d N /d S) ratios suggest purifying selection on protein-coding mitogenomic regions in all assessed lineages. CONCLUSIONS: We found no evidence of positive selection acting on mitochondrial protein-coding genes in either L. flavicauda or the broader genus Lagothrix; all analyses instead support pervasive purifying selection across genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation. These results suggest that unlike in some other non-human primates occupying high elevations, the adaptive response of L. flavicauda to living in the Andes does not appear to involve evolution in the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation pathway, and likely involves alternative genetic pathways or mechanisms not captured by mitochondrial sequence evolution. By providing the first publicly available high-coverage mitochondrial genome for L. flavicauda, this study establishes a foundation for future population mitogenomic investigations of adaptation, evolutionary history, and conservation in this Critically Endangered, high-altitude primate.
